a:r.a:t: This slide shows the data pipeline.

The data source is the EIA Open Data API, specifically weekly U.S. retail gasoline prices. The project also has a synthetic fallback for testing or local runs without an API key, but the final data snapshot uses the real EIA series.

After collection, the raw data is cleaned into a simple weekly table. The pipeline sorts by date, converts price values to numeric format, removes duplicate weeks, and saves a raw CSV snapshot. Keeping that raw snapshot is useful because the deployed API can serve forecasts from the same data version that the models were trained on.

For feature engineering, I keep the model frame intentionally explainable. The XGBoost model uses lag features at 1, 2, 4, 8, and 52 weeks. Those lags represent recent level, short-term momentum, and yearly seasonality. I also include month and ISO week features to represent calendar patterns.

This matters because gasoline prices have both short-term movement and seasonal structure. Rather than adding many hard-to-explain variables, I wanted a compact feature set that I could explain clearly during the presentation.
The final dataset contains 1,729 rows spanning April 5, 1993 through May 18, 2026.
